summary: Gives the overall framework for the data plane of Deterministic Networking (DetNet), which aims to carry time-sensitive traffic with bounded latency and very low loss. It covers concepts common to any DetNet data plane and touches on related controller plane considerations.

plainLanguage.summary: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is designed for flows that need very low loss and bounded delivery latency. This RFC explains the data-plane layers and the replication, elimination, routing, and resource-management functions they can use.

questions: what are detnet service and forwarding sub-layers
subtitle: A framework for DetNet data planes that support low loss and bounded delivery latency.

tldr.problem: Real-time flows may need very low packet loss and an assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency.
tldr.mechanism: DetNet separates service functions such as replication and duplicate elimination from forwarding functions such as resource allocation and explicit routing.
tldr.outcome: The memo provides common data-plane concepts and controller-plane considerations for IP and MPLS approaches. It is an Informational framework.

today: RFC 8938 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the memo provides a framework for DetNet data-plane specifications.

sections.title: DetNet Service Goals
sections.content:
DetNet provides a way to carry specified unicast or multicast flows for real-time applications with extremely low packet-loss rates and assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency. The framework covers data-plane concepts common to DetNet specifications and also discusses related controller-plane considerations.

The data plane is modeled as a service sub-layer and a forwarding sub-layer. The service sub-layer provides protection and reordering. The forwarding sub-layer uses traffic-engineering mechanisms for congestion protection, low loss, assured latency, and limited out-of-order delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet is intended for real-time flows that need low loss and bounded delivery time. It combines service-level protection with forwarding that manages paths and resources.

sections.title: Service and Forwarding Sub-Layers
sections.content:
The service sub-layer can sequence packets, replicate flows, encode packet information, eliminate duplicates, merge flows, and reorder packets. The forwarding sub-layer provides connectivity using explicit routes and allocated resources. A particular forwarding technology may provide capabilities that are not present in another technology.

The service layer may be carried directly by IP tunnels or MPLS, or may use an overlay where packets are carried natively between key nodes. DetNet can operate over IP or MPLS and can also use supporting sub-network technologies. IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking is an example of a possible underlying technology, but TSN support is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: The service sub-layer can protect a flow by making copies and handling their order. The forwarding sub-layer selects a route and assigns resources to carry the flow.

sections.title: Flow Identification and Packet Metadata
sections.content:
The data plane can carry a Flow-ID to identify a flow or aggregate, and a sequence number for packet replication, elimination, and ordering functions (PREOF). Metadata may be explicit in a dedicated header field or implicit in an existing field.

Native DetNet IP can use existing packet information for flow identification, while an IP encapsulation may be used when more metadata is needed. In DetNet MPLS, labels identify forwarding and service context; a DetNet control word may carry service metadata such as a sequence number. The memo leaves the exact encapsulation to the relevant data-plane specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets need enough information for the network to identify their flow and, when required, their sequence. IP and MPLS approaches carry this information in different ways.

sections.title: Resource Allocation, Paths, and Protection
sections.content:
Resources may be reserved for individual flows to reduce contention, loss, and jitter. Flows are expected to follow their reserved traffic profile; queuing, policing, and shaping can help prevent one misbehaving flow from compromising others. Explicit routes steer packets along paths associated with their allocated resources.

Service protection can send copies over multiple paths and eliminate duplicates at selected nodes. Reordering may require buffers and can add delay or jitter. The memo describes linear protection examples, notes that path-delay differences can exceed a function's buffering ability, and says packet-by-packet load sharing is not recommended unless PREOF is used to preserve protection and order.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet can reserve resources and select a specific route for a flow. Sending copies over different paths can improve protection, but the receiver must handle late or duplicate packets.

sections.title: Controller-Plane Responsibilities
sections.content:
The Controller Plane must be able to instantiate flows, determine explicit paths, reserve link bandwidth and node resources, coordinate queuing, manage bidirectional flows, support aggregation, advertise resources, and provision flow-identification information along a path.

These tasks can use distributed signaling, centralized management, or a hybrid approach. The memo says the methods may differ in scalability, resource optimization, and resilience even when they produce equivalent data-plane forwarding results. The detailed controller protocol and PREOF management are outside this framework's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller or set of protocols must configure the path, reserve resources, and tell each node how to identify the flow. The framework allows centralized, distributed, or combined control.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data plane must preserve data integrity and delivery of the DetNet service. Protection may come from the underlying technology, such as IPsec for IP flows or MACsec in an Ethernet sub-network. Controller-plane flow identification can reveal information about the traffic being managed.

Policing and shaping at a domain edge can limit excess traffic from malicious or malfunctioning devices. Authentication and authorization of devices within a DetNet domain can help mitigate attacks that delay packets. Edge controls can also limit flow escape into other networks.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet needs to protect both packet delivery and the control information that identifies flows. Edge policing and authenticated devices can reduce risks from excess traffic and unauthorized changes.
